clue.text: Commonwealth head supporting Cotter's reform

parts.note: to be pro something is to support it

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so the letters of the name are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A Lord's head stands up for a reformed peasant cottager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonwealth head' points to Cromwell, who ruled the English Commonwealth as Lord Protector; a cotter was a Scottish peasant tenant.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Cromwell, head of the English Commonwealth, held the title Lord Protector.

clue.text: Take uncle up, up to see the big cats

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are written from the bottom, so the run is turned round

parts.note: Uncle Sam is the personification of the USA
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trip with an uncle up to the zoo to view the lions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' (the second one) turns SAMUP round to read PUMAS; 'Take' and 'to see' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Pumas, also called cougars, are large wild felines of the Americas.

clue.text: Tiptree? (Unlikely to be found in Essex)

definitions.text: Tiptree? (Unlikely to be found in Essex)

parts.words: Tiptree? (Unlikely to be found in Essex)
parts.note: Tiptree is an Essex village, but split up it reads as a tree of tipping: to grease someone's palm is to tip or bribe them, and a tropical palm tree would hardly grow in Essex

explanation.surface: A query about an Essex village, with a parenthetical aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiptree is a village in Essex, England, famous for jam. Read 'tip tree', and 'oil the palm' means to bribe or tip.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropical tree yielding palm oil is, punningly, a tree for greasing someone's hand with a tip.

clue.text: Feast about to finish for a Londoner.

indicators.note: the festival's letters go round the other piece, so about signals a container here

parts.note: Easter is a Christian feast
to end is to finish

explanation.surface: Someone from London polishing off a banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the finishing word inside the feast, splitting it after its fourth letter. The East End is a traditionally working-class district of London.
explanation.definitionFit: An East Ender comes from the East End, the traditional working-class district of the capital.

clue.text: Can't let runs suffer, that's clear

indicators.note: letting the scoring rate suffer signals that these letters are damaged into a new order

explanation.surface: A cricket captain insists the run rate must not drop, plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffer' rearranges the eleven letters of CANT LET RUNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Translucent glass lets light pass through, so it is see-through, close to transparent.

clue.text: The box trade ?

parts.note: reads as the business of making boxes or of boxing, but a box was also a heavy overcoat, so the box trade is the clothing business, the old slang name for which uses a word for a scrap of cloth

explanation.surface: A question about the business of packaging, or of television.
explanation.walkthrough: The clothing industry is called the rag trade; a box coat was a heavy coachman's overcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Rag is the slang word in the phrase for the garment business, where cloth and clothing are made and sold.

clue.text: Money for a Post-Impressionist to make his mark, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken, so the spelling changes but the sound stays

parts.words: a Post-Impressionist to make his mark
parts.note: a post impressionist stamps letters: to frank mail is to mark it with postage paid

explanation.surface: Cash offered to a painter like Cézanne to help him make a name.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Post-Impressionist' as someone who impresses the post: franking a letter marks it. The French coin sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The franc was the currency of France, Belgium and Switzerland, among others.

clue.text: Support for Mr Facing-Both-Ways

parts.note: Mr Facing-both-ways in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is a waverer; the undecided are said to sit on a barrier between two fields

explanation.surface: Backing for a two-faced character from an old allegory.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Facing-both-ways is a character in Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress; someone who won't take sides 'sits on the fence'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence-sitter refuses to commit, so the barrier he perches on is what holds him up.

clue.text: Be a star turn, or in line with one

indicators.note: turn means the letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Advice to an actor: give a stellar performance, or stand in the chorus line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' rearranges BE A STAR; 'or' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking abreast means side by side, level with a companion.

clue.text: Not the victor's crown

parts.note: a loser is said to be knocked into a three-cornered hat, so this headgear is what the beaten side wears, not the laurel wreath

explanation.surface: A remark about what goes on the loser's head, not the winner's.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'knock into a cocked hat' is to defeat utterly; a cocked hat is an old tricorn.
explanation.definitionFit: The tricorn is ironically the headgear of the thoroughly beaten, from the idiom for an outright defeat.

clue.text: Poor Selima's a witch

indicators.note: poor suggests the name is in bad shape, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Pity Selima, who turns out to be a sorceress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges SELIMAS. Melissa is the good sorceress in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso.
explanation.definitionFit: Melissa is an enchantress in Ariosto's epic poem, a female magician.

clue.text: Information, boy, applying to any of the class

definitions.text: applying to any of the class

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
Eric is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad is briefed on something relevant to his whole school year.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Generic means general, true of every member of a group rather than one.

clue.text: Criticize roofing material

definitions.meaning: the grey stone split into thin tiles for roofs

explanation.surface: Run down the stuff on the roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: harsh criticism in British slang, and thin grey stone tiles laid on roofs.

clue.text: Egg eaters regroup when set apart

indicators.note: regroup says the letters gather again in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Diners eating eggs move to other tables when separated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regroup' rearranges EGG EATERS; 'when' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To segregate is to separate one group from others, keeping them isolated.

clue.text: The impression one gets, trying the sea-cook's pudding?

definitions.text: The impression one gets, trying the sea-cook's pudding?

parts.words: The impression one gets, trying the sea-cook's pudding?
parts.note: the proof of the pudding is in the eating, and a ship's kitchen is the galley; a printer's trial impression taken from type in a tray bears the same name

explanation.surface: What you feel when tasting the ship's cook's dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship's kitchen is the galley, and 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating'; in printing, a galley proof is a trial print.
explanation.definitionFit: Printers pull a first trial print from type set in a long tray, for checking before pages are made up.

clue.text: Light blue flower

parts.note: Cambridge's sporting colour is light blue, and a flower is something that flows, so a river of the Light Blues

explanation.surface: A pale blue bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridge University teams are the Light Blues; 'flower' is a crossword word for a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The river flowing through Cambridge, home of the Light Blues, is a 'flower' in the sense of something that flows.

clue.text: He sets out about fifty to convert Germany

definitions.text: He sets out about fifty to convert Germany

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

indicators.note: to convert something is to change its form, so these letters change their order

explanation.surface: A missionary sets off around AD 50 to bring the Germans to Christianity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to convert' signals the anagram of Germany; read as a whole, the clue also pictures a missionary priest setting out around AD 50.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister of religion is the sort of person who sets out to convert a nation.

clue.text: Incomprehensible suggestion of 3's bigamy

definitions.meaning: gibberish, a language one cannot follow
in Cockney slang a wife is 'my old Dutch', so a Londoner from 3-down with two wives would have two of them

explanation.surface: Gibberish hints at a Cockney's having two wives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife (from 'duchess'), and 3-down is the Londoner. Double Dutch is also a skipping game.
explanation.definitionFit: Double Dutch is talk that cannot be understood, and punningly two wives for a Cockney.

clue.text: All atremble, I'd turn on the pugilists

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means this piece is placed above the rest
turn means these two letters are turned round to read the other way

parts.note: the contraction of I would, two letters
taken as written
the ring is boxing and its fighters as a whole

explanation.surface: Shaking with nerves, I'd round on the boxers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' makes DI from I'D; THE RING is the boxing world collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shaking with indecision or nerves is quivering and hesitant.

clue.text: Making do with ten men, possibly, outside strength

indicators.note: the shuffled letters sit outside the other piece, around it
possibly says the letters might be arranged some other way

parts.note: force is strength or power

explanation.surface: A football side forced to play with only ten men, but strong despite that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges TEN MEN into ENMENT, which goes 'outside' FORCE; 'with' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Enforcement is compelling someone to obey, literally making them carry out an action.

clue.text: "In their —— cups freshly remember'd" (Henry V)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from the St Crispin's Day speech in Shakespeare's history play, where the deeds of the band of brothers will be toasted

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's St Crispin's Day speech with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Henry V is 'Be in their flowing cups freshly remember'd'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes cups brimming over with wine at future feasts.

clue.text: This man never appears weather-beaten

parts.note: the forecaster from the meteorological office is a weatherman, so one might expect him to look battered by the elements

explanation.surface: A man who always looks fresh, however wild the elements.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met Office is Britain's national weather service, and its forecaster is a Met man.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for meteorological, the word names the national weather service and its forecasters.

clue.text: Drink produced by illegal army ?

parts.note: produced means made
the IRA is the outlawed Irish Republican Army

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a beverage was made by paramilitaries.
explanation.walkthrough: IRA is the Irish Republican Army; 'by' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeira is a fortified wine from the Portuguese Atlantic island of that name.

clue.text: Stupid person backing favourites in March?

parts.note: a goose is a silly person

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is turned round

parts.note: pets are favourites, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A fool backing the favourites at the spring race meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' signals the reversal. The surface suggests betting at spring race meetings; 'March' is really the noun, a style of military parading.
explanation.definitionFit: The goose-step is a stiff-legged military marching style.

clue.text: What's left of the fire in 18's clue

definitions.text: What's left of the fire in 18's clue

parts.words: What's left of the fire in 18's clue
parts.note: the glowing remnant of a fire is found buried in the apostrophised word near the end of the 18-down quotation

explanation.surface: A request to find the fire's remains within another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Look inside the word 'remember'd' in the 18-down clue, after its first two letters, to find the remnant.
explanation.definitionFit: A glowing coal is what remains of a burnt-out fire.

clue.text: Generously supply three quarters about the same

indicators.note: about tells us the compass letters go around the other piece

parts.note: east, north and west are three of the compass's four quarters
do is short for ditto, meaning the same

explanation.surface: Give lavishly to three-quarters of the population, roughly the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts DO (ditto, 'the same') inside E, N, W, three of the four compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow is to give money or a lasting gift, as to a college.

clue.text: Bought someone a drink in turn, say

indicators.note: say means we hear the word, so it is spelt differently but sounds the same

parts.note: to wind a handle is to turn it

explanation.surface: Took turns buying rounds of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: WIND as in winding a clock rhymes with 'mind', so it sounds the same; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To be wined and dined is to be treated to drinks and a meal by a host.

clue.text: Old transvestite, we hear, holds the post

indicators.note: we hear means the words are spoken, sounding the same but spelt otherwise

parts.note: an old bag is a nasty old woman, so a man dressed as one is a male bag

explanation.surface: An elderly cross-dresser keeps hold of his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bag' is slang for an unpleasant old woman, so a male one is an old transvestite.
explanation.definitionFit: A sack carried by postmen contains the letters and parcels.

clue.text: Set to give a leg up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is written from the bottom, so it reads backwards

explanation.surface: Ready to give someone a boost over a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns LEG round in this down clue; 'to give a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Jelly that has set has firmed up, as to gel is to solidify.

clue.text: Owing (in two words) to the view

parts.note: the first letter of the word, split off as its own word
split off the first letter and the rest is wing, and a pinion is a bird's wing

explanation.surface: Indebted, as I'll put it in two words, to your point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket tells us to read 'Owing' as two words, O WING, and PINION is another word for a wing.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion is a view or belief held about something.

clue.text: Current return re Geneva ?

indicators.note: return means turned back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
geneva is an old name for Dutch gin

explanation.surface: Correspondence replying about the Swiss city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns REGIN round to NIGER. Geneva (or genever) is Dutch gin; the Niger is a West African river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is a flowing current of water, and the Niger is a great West African one.

clue.text: Military 1 ac on the beach

parts.note: 1-across is a protector or guard; the Household Cavalry has a mounted regiment of that name, and the same title is worn by a swimmer's rescuer at the seaside

explanation.surface: A soldier guarding the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Life Guards are a British cavalry regiment; on the beach a lifeguard watches over bathers.
explanation.definitionFit: A guard who protects lives can be a cavalryman of the Household regiment or a beach rescuer.
